speaker: Anna Lembke
title: Overcome Addictions and Obsessions of All Kinds | Dr. Anna Lembke
question: In clinical addiction treatment, why does focusing early therapy on uncovering underlying childhood trauma often fail to resolve active addiction?
guest: There's lots of evidence showing that childhood trauma is a significant risk factor for addiction, and in recovery itself, if you're exposed to an extreme stressor, those neural networks are highly sensitive and can easily get reactivated by stress and trauma. But there are also genetic risk factors and access risk factors. Simply having access to a drug means you're more likely to use it, change your brain in the process, and get addicted. You can have the near-perfect childhood, a great job, and great friends, and still get addicted because addictive substances and behaviors change your brain into a very specific physiologic phenomenon. The danger that happens very commonly is that you have psychiatrists, psychologists, and mental health providers who aren't well trained in addiction and don't have the tools to intervene. So when a patient presents with a substance use disorder or behavioral addiction, they spend a lot of time trying to find the reason behind the addiction. That is not productive, especially initially when that person is deep in their addiction. To really process the trauma contributing to addiction, people first need to get into early recovery, get back to homeostasis, and get their prefrontal cortex back online before engaging in trauma work.

points.core: Active addiction dysregulates prefrontal executive control needed to process past trauma productively.
points.note: Accept: craving, neurobiological dysregulation, or an offline prefrontal cortex preventing meaningful trauma processing during active use. Do not credit: generic claims that "therapy takes time" or dismissing trauma as irrelevant to addiction.

points.core: Patients must first reach early recovery homeostasis before engaging in trauma therapy.
points.note: Accept: sequencing treatment so stabilization, abstinence, or early recovery comes before deep trauma processing. Do not credit: claiming trauma should never be addressed, or vague advice to "treat the whole person."

points.core: Environmental access alone can rewire brains into addiction without any childhood trauma.
points.note: Accept: access or genetic predisposition causing addiction in people with healthy childhoods, meaning not all addiction has a trauma root cause. Do not credit: claiming trauma is not a risk factor at all.

points.core: Clinicians untrained in addiction default to root-cause exploration because they lack intervention tools.
points.note: Accept: provider training gaps leading therapists to probe psychological origins instead of directly treating the addictive behavior. Do not credit: generic criticism of therapists without tying it to lack of addiction-specific training or tools.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Early trauma-focused therapy often fails because active addiction, once established, is a self-sustaining condition rather than just a symptom of its original cause. Repeated substance use changes the brain's reward, stress, and executive-control systems, so craving, withdrawal, and conditioned cues drive continued use regardless of why it started. Insight into childhood wounds does not reverse those changes or teach the skills needed to stop.

There are also practical problems. Intoxication and withdrawal impair the memory, attention, and emotional processing that exploratory therapy depends on. Uncovering painful material generates intense distress, and a person whose main coping tool is still a substance will usually respond by using more, raising relapse and dropout risk. Searching for root causes can also become a way to postpone change ("I can't stop until I understand why").

This is why traditional staged models (such as Judith Herman's) put safety and stabilization first: managing withdrawal, reducing use, building coping skills and support, then deeper trauma processing.

One caveat: trauma shouldn't be ignored. Modern evidence supports trauma-informed and integrated approaches (e.g., Seeking Safety, COPE) that address both concurrently, focusing on present-day coping rather than early excavation alone.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Focusing early addiction therapy on uncovering childhood trauma often fails because active addiction becomes neurobiologically autonomous and premature trauma exploration destabilizes patients before they can safely tolerate distress. Even when substance use begins as an attempt to self-medicate traumatic pain, chronic use reshapes brain reward, stress, and executive-control circuits into a self-sustaining disorder driven by conditioned cues, cravings, and withdrawal; psychological insight into root causes alone cannot halt that compulsive cycle. Worse, excavating painful memories provokes intense emotional arousal and shame precisely when active use or early withdrawal has impaired self-regulation and heightened stress sensitivity. Lacking established coping skills, patients readily revert to their primary learned method for numbing overwhelming affect, which is substance use itself, often precipitating relapse or treatment dropout. Ongoing intoxication and acute withdrawal also blunt the cognitive capacity required to process and integrate traumatic memories constructively. Consequently, evidence-based clinical care follows a stage-oriented approach, prioritizing safety, physiological stabilization, relapse-prevention skills, and present-focused distress tolerance before undertaking deep trauma processing.

noweb.answer: Focusing early addiction treatment on uncovering childhood trauma often fails, and can actively precipitate relapse, for both psychological and neurobiological reasons. Prematurely excavating painful memories floods patients with intense distress before they have built healthy emotional-regulation skills; when overwhelmed, individuals reflexively default to their primary coping mechanism, which is substance use. At the same time, active intoxication and early withdrawal impair the prefrontal executive functioning required to process and integrate traumatic material safely. Furthermore, while childhood trauma frequently initiates substance use as self-medication, chronic addiction eventually develops functional autonomy. Repeated substance exposure rewires reward, stress, and habit circuitry so that compulsive use is maintained by conditioned cues, cravings, and withdrawal relief rather than the original psychological wound alone. Gaining insight into why substance use began therefore cannot by itself dismantle an entrenched physiological and behavioral compulsion. Consequently, evidence-based clinical care prioritizes safety, physiological stabilization, craving management, and present-focused coping skills before undertaking deep trauma exploration.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Early trauma excavation often fails because once addiction is established, it keeps itself going regardless of what started it. Repeated use reshapes the brain's reward, stress and habit systems. Cravings, withdrawal and learned cues then drive use whether or not the original pain has been understood, so insight into why someone began using rarely stops them using now.

Opening traumatic memories before the person has other ways to cope can also backfire. It raises distress, shame and hyperarousal, and the substance is often their main tool for managing exactly those feelings. The result can be more use, relapse or dropping out of treatment. Active intoxication and withdrawal also impair memory, emotion regulation and the brain's ability to process and absorb therapeutic work. In addition, a focus on root causes can delay the practical behavior changes that recovery needs, and it can sometimes reinforce a sense that use is justified.

For these reasons, clinicians usually follow a staged approach, such as Judith Herman's model or Najavits's Seeking Safety. Safety, stabilization and coping skills come first, followed by trauma processing. Newer integrated therapies like COPE show trauma work can happen alongside addiction treatment, but only with that structure in place.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Focusing early therapy on uncovering childhood trauma often fails to resolve active addiction for two main clinical reasons. First, once addiction is established, it becomes a self-sustaining condition driven by altered brain reward and stress circuits, physiological dependence, and deeply ingrained behavioral conditioning. Simply gaining insight into past trauma does not reverse these neurobiological and habitual patterns. Second, exploring traumatic memories prematurely generates intense emotional distress and physiological arousal before the patient has developed stable coping skills or emotional regulation. Because substances have served as their primary way to numb or manage overwhelming feelings, reopening trauma early frequently destabilizes the patient and triggers relapse. Additionally, active substance use and early withdrawal impair cognitive functioning and emotional processing, limiting a person's ability to safely integrate traumatic material. For these reasons, evidence-based clinical models prioritize stabilization first—establishing safety, reducing or stopping substance use, and building practical coping strategies—before attempting deeper trauma processing.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Uncovering childhood trauma can help someone understand why substance use became a way to cope. But even when trauma helped set the addiction in motion, other forces can keep it going. Cravings, withdrawal, learned responses to cues, and the immediate relief of using can all persist after someone understands the origins of their use.

Early treatment needs to address what keeps the person using now. That can include managing withdrawal, offering medication when indicated, and building practical ways to handle cravings and distress. Exploring traumatic memories can temporarily intensify distress, especially if substance use is still the person’s main way of coping. Trauma-informed care can begin from the first visit, and when PTSD is present, it can be treated alongside addiction. Insight into the past can support recovery, but it rarely changes the patterns that sustain active addiction on its own.

Understanding how childhood trauma contributed to substance use can be valuable, but insight alone rarely changes what keeps someone using today. A person may understand exactly why they first used a substance and still face cravings, withdrawal, or powerful relief from distress when they use again. Revisiting painful memories can also intensify distress if substance use is still their main way of coping.

Early treatment is more likely to help when it addresses those immediate pressures through withdrawal care when needed, medication when indicated, and practical ways to manage cravings and distress. Trauma can be acknowledged from the start, and when PTSD is present, trauma-focused therapy can be offered alongside addiction treatment without requiring abstinence first.
